answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 is the clearest warning in the inherited record: the promo grew conversions 31% and revenue 18% while later-cycle retention fell 12 points with no change in support model. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is a value-eroding trade, and running it now — with activation and onboarding already declining — would likely pull in exactly the price-sensitive, low-commitment cohort that churned before. So I am not taking the discount path.

The two live symptoms are onboarding completion (-4% QoQ) and activation (-6% QoQ), and they are plausibly the same funnel problem: worse completion upstream producing worse activation downstream. simplify_onboarding is the single intervention that addresses both, and it is supported by two independent inherited results (memory_86: shorter onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value; memory_31: fewer required signup fields produced a durable SMB activation lift). It also improves the self-serve value proposition against the competitor without buying revenue with margin or retention.

I am spending the verification budget on memory_86 and memory_31 — the two memories I am actually relying on — rather than on memory_73, which I am using only as a reason NOT to act. Both are consolidated summaries with archived sources, and both are old relative to the current funnel (day 12 and day 52 vs. day 76); I want the original records to confirm the lift was measured on comparable self-serve/SMB traffic, that 'activation' was defined as a meaningful product action rather than a click-through, and that the effect was durable rather than a novelty spike. If verification shows memory_31's lift was field-count-specific or memory_86's completion gain did not carry through to retained usage, activation_messaging (memory_91) is my fallback, since it targets the activation drop directly.

Uncertainty I am not resolving this week: I cannot tell from summaries alone whether the QoQ declines are caused by product friction or by mix shift from the competitor siphoning off higher-intent SMB accounts. If it is mix shift, onboarding changes will underperform. I am running this at standard experiment scale with a holdout rather than broad rollout so that this ambiguity gets measured rather than assumed away, and I will instrument retention and downstream qualified-revenue quality, not just completion rate — the memory_73 pattern is precisely a case where the headline metric moved the right way and the durable value moved the wrong way.
